source_abstract: The KPLANT database is a global compilation of whole-plant hydraulic conductance (kplant) measurements, providing harmonised data on plant water transport capacity along the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. The database contains 3,873 observations from 356 datasets, covering 429 species across 245 genera and 100 families, sampled on six continents and seven plant growth forms (tree, shrub, liana, graminoid, forb, stem succulent, fern), spanning 1970 to the present. kplant values are provided as originally reported and additionally standardised on five normalisation bases (leaf area, sapwood area, wood area, ground area, and whole-plant), together with the underlying water flux and water potential measurements, plant- and stand-level characteristics, and metadata on site, experimental conditions, and source publication. This deposit contains: KPLANT_database.csv - main database with all kplant observations and metadata. Extraction_template.xlsx - standardised template used for data extraction. Individual_datasets.zip - compressed zip file containing the per-study .xlsx datasets. Qc_reports.zip - compressed zip file containing the HTML quality-control reports for individual datasets. Variable definitions, units, and full methodological details are provided in the accompanying data descriptor (Zhao, Mencuccini, et al., Flo. KPLANT: a global database of plant water transport capacity. Scientific Data</em>, in preparation). Code used to build the database and to generate figures and the technical validation analyses is available at  https://github.com/vflo/Kplant_database . The automated quality-control procedure used to produce the reports in <code>Qc_reports/</code> is available at  https://github.com/vflo/Kwp_QC .

source_title: Functional traits of charophytes to compare vascular and non-vascular leaf traits.
source_authors: Dalla Vecchia, Alice; Bolpagni, Rossano; Azzella, Mattia Martin
source_subjects: Characeae; freshwater; functional traits; leaf economics spectrum
source_abstract: This dataset includes functional trait data measured on leaf-like structures of 9 charophyte species: Chara aculeolata Kützing, C. aspera Willdenow, C. globularis Thuillier, C. papillosa Kützing, C. tomentosa Linnaeus, C. vulgaris Linnaeus, Nitella flexilis (Linnaeus) C. Agardh, N. hyalina (De Candolle) C. Agardh and Nitellopsis obtusa (Desvaux) J. Groves. The data supports the article "A standardized protocol and basic ecological findings to include charophytes in functional trait studies", abstract: Background and Scope. Charophytes comprise key benthic macroalgae that play multiple ecological roles in freshwater. Despite this, they are excluded from community-level functional trait research, leading to an underestimation of functional diversity of charophyte-dominated ecosystems. This study aims to develop a standardized protocol for measuring leaf functional traits for charophytes, and to provide a first functional comparison between charophytes and common vascular macrophyte life forms. Methods. Functional units were identified that perform the leaf function and reflect the modular growth of charophytes (whorls, branchlets, and internodes). Leaf (branchlet) area, specific leaf area, leaf dry matter content, chlorophylls, carotenoids, phosphorus, nitrogen and carbon content were measured on 9 charophyte species. The protocol was validated by comparing traits between charophytes and 5 macrophyte groups (lemnids, nymphaeids, submerged-broad-leaf, submerged-narrow-leaf, and utricularids), using a multidimensional niche approach. Key Results. Trait measurements were comparable between charophytes and vascular macrophytes. Charophytes’ functional traits showed alignment with ecological expectations, such as increased specific leaf area and reduced dry matter content along the expected growth depth. Overall, charophytes showed high intraspecific variability, attributable to their ability to grow across wide gradients of depth and light. Charophyte functional niche overlapped mostly with submerged narrow-leaved plants but maintained >40% niche uniqueness. Conclusions. Charophytes expand the functional space occupied by macrophytes, contributing to understanding the overall functional diversity of aquatic plants. Following research should apply the protocol to all genera of the family Characeae and investigate the environmental drivers of trait variability.

source_title: Burn hot or tolerate trees: flammability decreases with shade tolerance in grasses
source_authors: Gao, Xiulin; Schwilk, Dylan
source_subjects: fire; grass; flammability; shade tolerance; post-fire response; ecological strategy
source_abstract: In ecosystems where trees and grasses coexist, some grass species are found only in open habitats and others persist under trees. The persistence of shade intolerant grasses in ecosystems such as open woodlands and savannas depends on recurrent fires to open the tree canopy. Therefore, grasses that depend on open sites might benefit from high flammability. We tested if shade intolerant grasses are more flammable than shade tolerant grasses and if flammability differences affected post-fire grass growth. We examined the relationship between shade tolerance and flammability by determining individual-level flammability and species shade tolerance of 17 grass species. We also measured grass traits to determine trait effects on flammability and the post-fire response. Grass species varied in flammability, mainly in the amount of heat produced during burning. Shade tolerant species produced less heat at 50 cm above the ground. Biomass and live fuel moisture had the greatest effects on heat release. However, the negative effect of live fuel moisture on heat release at the soil surface was weakened in plants with high specific leaf area. In addition, grass bulk density negatively influenced heat release at 50 cm height. Heat release at the soil surface negatively influenced post-fire growth. However, the influences of soil heating and species-specific traits on individual survival were more complex with 2- and 3-way interactions. Shade tolerance was negatively correlated with a major axis of flammability variation: shade tolerant grasses produced less heat where that heat could damage tree boles. Such heterogeneity in grass flammability may help maintain the tree-grass mixture in natural plant communities. If shade tolerant grasses near trees cause less fire damage to woody plants, especially tree saplings, this may weaken positive grass-fire feedbacks and thus aid the long-term coexistence of trees and grasses.

source_title: Data from: Different-sized grazers have distinctive effects on plant functional composition of an African savannah
source_authors: van der Plas, Fons; Howison, Ruth A.; Mpanza, Nokukhanya; Cromsigt, Joris P. G. M.; Olff, Han
source_subjects: plant–herbivore interactions; mesoherbivores; savannah; white rhino; bunch grass; grazing lawns
source_abstract: Grazing ungulates play a key role in many ecosystems worldwide and can form diverse assemblages, such as in African savannahs. In many of these ecosystems, present-day ungulate communities are impoverished subsets of once diverse assemblages. While we know that excluding all ungulates from grasslands can exert major effects on both the structure and composition of the vegetation, how different individual ungulate species may have contrasting effects on grassland communities remains poorly understood. Here, we performed a long term "Russian doll" grazing exclosure experiment in an African savannah to test for the effects of different size classes of grazers on grassland structure and composition. At five sites, grazer species of decreasing size class (ranging from white rhino to scrub hare) were excluded using four fence types, to experimentally create different realized grazer assemblages. The vegetation structure and the grass functional community composition were characterized in six different years over a 10 year period. Additionally, animal footprints were counted to quantify the abundance of different ungulate species in each treatment. We found that while vegetation height was mostly driven by total grazing pressure of all species together, ungulate community composition best explained the functional community composition of grasses. In the short term, smaller ungulate species ('mesoherbivores') had strongest effects on vegetation composition, by shifting communities towards dominance by species with low specific leaf area and low nutritional value. In the long term, large grazers had stronger but similar effects on the functional composition of the system. Surprisingly, the largest 'mega-herbivore', white rhinoceros, did not have strong effects on the vegetation structure or composition. Synthesis. Our results support the idea that different size classes of grazers have varying effects on the functional composition of grassland plant communities. Therefore, the worldwide decline in the diversity of ungulate species is expected to have (had) major impacts on community composition and functioning of grassland ecosystems, even if total grazing pressure has remained constant, e.g., due to replacement by livestock.

source_title: Data from: Positive associations with native shrubs are intense and important for an exotic invader but not the native annual community across an aridity gradient
source_authors: Lucero, Jacob; Seifan, Merav; Callaway, Ragan; Lortie, Christopher
source_subjects: Bromus rubens; deserts; environmental gradients; positive interactions; shrubs; Stress-gradient hypothesis
source_abstract: AIM AND LOCATION: Positive interactions influence the assembly of plant communities globally, particularly in stressful environments like deserts.  However, few studies have measured the intensity and relative importance of positive interactions involving native and invasive species along aridity gradients.  These measures are essential for predicting how dryland communities will respond to biological invasions and environmental change.  Here, we measured the intensity and importance of positive associations formed between native shrubs and the annual plant community, which included highly invasive Bromus madritensis ssp. rubens (" B. rubens ") and native neighbours, along an aridity gradient across the Mojave and San Joaquin Deserts. METHODS: Along the gradient, we sampled metrics of abundance and performance for invasive B. rubens , native annual species (pooled), exotic annual species (pooled), and all annual species (pooled) during peak flowering at 120 pairs of shrub and open microsites. RESULTS: Across the gradient, B. rubens occurred at far greater abundance, cover, biomass, and fitness near shrubs than away from shrubs.  When Larrea tridentata was the focal shrub, positive effects on B. rubens abundance and cover were weakest (though never negative) at the most arid sites under the shortest shrubs.  The native annual community occurred at greater abundance, cover, and species richness away from shrubs, regardless of relative aridity or shrub traits.  Community-level species richness was greatest away from shrubs, but exotic species richness was similar in shrub and open microsites. MAIN CONCLUSIONS: Across two deserts,  B. rubens formed intense and important positive associations with native shrubs that consistently imporoved its abundance, cover, biomass, and fitness; and for abundance and cover, the intensity of  B. rubens - L. tridentata   associations depended upon relative aridity and shrub height.  By strongly facilitating a dominant invader but not native- or community-level biodiversity, native shrubs provided the wrong kind of help to the annual plant community.

source_abstract: AIM AND LOCATION: Positive interactions influence the assembly of plant communities globally, particularly in stressful environments like deserts.  However, few studies have measured the intensity and relative importance of positive interactions involving native and invasive species along aridity gradients.  These measures are essential for predicting how dryland communities will respond to biological invasions and environmental change.  Here, we measured the intensity and importance of positive associations formed between native shrubs and the annual plant community, which included highly invasive Bromus madritensis ssp. rubens (" B. rubens ") and native neighbours, along an aridity gradient across the Mojave and San Joaquin Deserts. METHODS: Along the gradient, we sampled metrics of abundance and performance for invasive B. rubens , native annual species (pooled), exotic annual species (pooled), and all annual species (pooled) during peak flowering at 120 pairs of shrub and open microsites. RESULTS: Across the gradient, B. rubens occurred at far greater abundance, cover, biomass, and fitness near shrubs than away from shrubs.  When Larrea tridentata was the focal shrub, positive effects on B. rubens abundance and cover were weakest (though never negative) at the most arid sites under the shortest shrubs.  The native annual community occurred at greater abundance, cover, and species richness away from shrubs, regardless of relative aridity or shrub traits.  Community-level species richness was greatest away from shrubs, but exotic species richness was similar in shrub and open microsites. MAIN CONCLUSIONS: Across two deserts,  B. rubens formed intense and important positive associations with native shrubs that consistently imporoved its abundance, cover, biomass, and fitness; and for abundance and cover, the intensity of  B. rubens - L. tridentata   associations depended upon relative aridity and shrub height.  By strongly facilitating a dominant invader but not native- or community-level biodiversity, native shrubs provided the wrong kind of help to the annual plant community.

source_title: Grazing lawns and overgrazing in frequently grazed grass communities
source_authors: Hempson, Gareth; Parr, Kate; Lehmann, Caroline; Archibald, Sally
source_subjects: degradation; environmental constraints; grass traits; growth forms; palatability; species composition; Poaceae
source_abstract: Frequent grazing can establish high forage value grazing lawns supporting high grazer densities, but can also produce overgrazed grass communities with unpalatable or low grass basal cover, supporting few grazers. Attempts to create grazing lawns via concentrated grazing, with a goal to increase grazer numbers, are thus risky without knowing how environmental conditions influence the likelihood of each outcome. We collected grass species and trait data from 33 frequently grazed grass communities across eastern South Africa (28 sites) and the Serengeti National Park, Tanzania (5 sites), covering wide rainfall (336–987 mm.yr-1) and soil (e.g. 44–93% sand) gradients. We identified four grass growth forms using hierarchical clustering on principal components analyses of trait data, and assessed trait-environment and growth form-environment relationships using fourth corner and principal components analyses. We distinguished two palatable grass growth forms that both attract yet resist grazers, and comprise grazing lawns: 1) 'lateral attractors' that spread vegetatively via stolons and rhizomes, and 2) 'tufted attractors' that form isolated tufts, and may have alternate tall growth forms. By contrast, 3) tough, upright, tufted 'resisters', and 4) 'avoiders' with sparse architectures or that grow appressed to the soil surface, are of little forage value and avoided by grazers. Grazing lawns occurred across a wide range of conditions, typically comprising lateral attractor grasses in drier, sandy environments, and tufted attractor grasses in wetter, low-sand environments. Resisters occurred on clay-rich soils in mesic areas, while avoiders were widespread but scarce. While grazing lawns can be established under most conditions, monitoring their composition and cover is important, as the potential for overgrazing seems as widely relevant. Tufted attractor-dominated lawns appear somewhat more vulnerable to degradation than lateral attractor-dominated lawns. Increased avoider or resister abundance both reduce forage value, although resisters may provide better soil protection.

source_title: The one hundred tree species prioritized for planting in the tropics and subtropics as indicated by database mining: standardization of 830 prioritized species to World Flora Online version 2023.12
source_authors: Kindt, Roeland
source_abstract: The  GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (GlobUNT; https://patspo.shinyapps.io/GlobalUsefulTrees/ ; Kindt et al. 2023 ) allows users to filter native useful tree species for any country in the world. One of the filters in this database refers to the The one hundred tree species prioritized for planting in the tropics and subtropics as indicated by database mining (Kindt et al. 2021 ). A version of GlobUNT will be released in 2026 that includes all 830 species listed in the prioritized list, whereas not all species were included in older versions.   This archive provides standardizations to the same taxonomic backbone of World Flora Online (Borsch et al. 2020 ; taxonomic backbone version 2023.12; Kindt 2020 ) as used for standardizations included in GlobUNT. It is also the same taxonomic backbone, and the same standardization protocols, that were used for the 2025 update of the Agroforestry Species Switchboard (Kindt et al. 2025 ). Hence crosslinking to databases listed in the Switchboard to obtain details for species of interest should be straightforward; a direct hyperlink to the Switchboard is also included in the archive. One of the columns in the archive indicates whether information on the environmental distribution of a species is available from the TreeGOER (Kindt 2023 ; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7922927 ) or TreeGOER+ ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11208040 ) databases.   References Kindt, R., Graudal, L., Lillesø, JP.B. et al. source_title: Edible Balcony Gardens for Retrofit - Vertical Garden Systems for Cities - Raw Data
source_authors: Spörl, Philipp; Brandl, Martin; Posnicek, Thomas; Pitha, Ulrike
source_subjects: Vertical Greening System; green balcony; retrofit of buildings; building greenery
source_abstract: Initial Situation, Challenges, and Motivation In social  housing , there are often deficits in terms of private outdoor space and opportunities for active greening and self-sufficiency . Existing buildings typically provide only limited exterior spaces and contribute little to improving the microclimate or local food production . Given the growing importance of sustainable resource use , climate adaptation , and social quality of life , there is a need for innovative concepts that can be retroactively implemented in existing buildings to generate ecological and social benefits . The objective is to create multifunctional , cost-effective , and sustainable outdoor spaces th ose directly engage residents and have ecological impact.   Objectives and Innovation   The project investigated the retroactive creation of apartment-related outdoor space with opportunities for self-gardening in social housing, considering sustainable rainwater irrigation. At a building requiring renovation, balconies were equipped with vertical planting systems for vegetables, fruits, and herbs. These outdoor spaces simultaneously serve as retreat and recreational areas, microclimate-enhancing building components, and productive horticultural infrastructure, enabling year-round, local food production on a limited footprint.   Methodology   To evaluate vertical green ery and its effects on user experience, productivity, and microclimate, a comprehensive measurement concept was developed for three sites, including two functional prototypes and one demonstration building. The core of data collection was sensor-based monitoring of climate, substrate, and water, capturing air temperature, humidity, thermal transfer, solar radiation, and water balance. Additionally, visually assessable parameters such as plant appearance and measurable parameters such as plant volume and biomass yield were systematically recorded.   Results   The results indicate that the examined vertical green ing systems have significant potential as multifunctional elements for building green ery and urban food production. Success factors include site-specific planning, appropriate plant selection, optimized planting density, reliable irrigation, and clearly defined objectives (e.g. yield, shading, privacy). For users without prior experience, low-maintenance and perennial plants are recommended. Initial guidance and support during the early phase help ensure proper plant care, irrigation, and harvesting, fostering stable vegetation development.   Conclusion and Outlook   Vertical greening systems are a promising tool for improving the microclimate, supporting urban food production, and enhancing the ecological and functional quality of buildings. For future applications and research, long-term monitoring is recommended to identify optimization potential in terms of energy efficiency, plant selection, yield, and microclimatic effects. Site-adapted plant selection, module positioning, and planting density are key parameters for successful implementation. The findings demonstrate that, with careful planning and management, vertical greening systems can generate sustainable benefits for residents and the urban microclimate.      - GERMAN VERSION -  Ausgangssituation , Problematik und Motivation   Im sozialen Wohnbau bestehen häufig Defizite hinsichtlich wohnungsbezogener Freiräume sowie Möglichkeiten zur aktiven Begrünung und Selbstversorgung . Bestehende Gebäude bieten meist nur begrenzte Außenräume und leisten nur einen geringen Beitrag zur Verbesserung des Mikroklimas oder zur lokalen Lebensmittelproduktion. Angesichts der zunehmenden Relevanz nachhaltiger Ressourcennutzung, Klimaanpassung und sozialer Lebensqualität besteht ein Bedarf an innovativen Konzepten, die nachträglich in Bestandsgebäuden implementiert werden können, um ökologische und soziale Mehrwerte zu generieren. Ziel ist es, multifunktionale, kosteneffiziente und nachhaltige Außenräume zu schaffen, die die Bewohner:innen direkt einbe ziehen und ökologisch wirksam sind.   Ziele und Innovationsgehalt   Das Projekt untersuchte die nachträgliche Schaffung von wohnungsbezogenem Freiraum mit Selbstgärtner :innen -Möglichkeiten im sozialen Wohnbau, unter Berücksichtigung einer nachhaltigen Regenwasserbewässerung. An einem sanierungsbedürftigen Bestandsgebäude wurden Balkone mit vertikalen Pflanzsystemen für Gemüse, Obst und Kräuter installiert. Die so geschaffenen Außenräume dienen gleichzeitig als Rückzugs- und Erholungsbereiche, mikroklimawirksame Bauteile und produktive gärtnerische Infrastruktur, wodurch eine ganzjährige, lokale Produktion von Lebensmittel n auf begrenzter Fläche ermöglicht wird.   Methodische Vorgehensweise   Zur Evaluation der Vertikalbegrünung und ihrer Wirkung auf Aufenthaltsqualität, Produktivität und Mikroklima wurde ein umfassendes Messkonzept für drei Standorte entwickelt , darunter zwei Funktionsmuster und ein Demonstrationsobjekt. Kern der Datenerhebung war ein sensorgestütztes Monitoring von Klima, Substrat und Wasser, einschließlich Lufttemperatur, Luftfeuchtigkeit, Wärmedurchgang, solarer Strahlung und Wasserbilanz. Ergänzend wurden visuell bestimmbare Parameter an den Pflanzen wie Erscheinungsbild, sowie messbare Parameter wie Pflanzenvolumen und Biomasseertrag systematisch erfasst.   Ergebnisse   Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die untersuchten Vertikalbegrünungssysteme ein großes Potenzial als multifunktionale Elemente für Gebäudebegrünung und urbane Lebensmittelproduktion besitzen. Erfolgsfaktoren sind standortangepasste Planung, Pflanzenauswahl, abgestimmte Pflanzdichte, zuverlässige Bewässerung und eine klare Definition der Zielsetzungen (z. B. Ertrag, Beschattung, Sichtschutz). Für Nutzer:innen ohne Vorerfahrung eignen sich pflegeleichte, ausdauernde Pflanzen. Eine begleitende Betreuung in der Anfangsphase unterstützt die Pflanzenpflege, Bewässerung und Ernte und fördert eine stabile Vegetationsentwicklung.   Schlussfolgerung und Ausblick   Vertikalbegrünungssysteme stellen ein vielversprechendes Instrument zur Verbesserung des Mikroklimas, zur Förderung urbaner Lebensmittelproduktion und zur Steigerung der ökologischen sowie funktionalen Qualität von Gebäuden dar. Für zukünftige Anwendungen und Forschungsprojekte ist eine langfristige Beobachtung empfehlenswert, um Optimierungspotenziale in Bezug auf Energieeffizienz, Pflanzenwahl, Ertrag und Mikroklimawirkung zu identifizieren. Standortangepasste Pflanzenauswahl, Modulpositionierung und Pflanzdichte sind zentrale Parameter für eine erfolgreiche Umsetzung. Die Ergebnisse belegen, dass Vertikalbegrünungssysteme bei sorgfältiger Planung und Betreuung nachhaltige Mehrwerte für Bewohner:innen und städtisches Mikroklima generieren können.

source_title: RiceMind Dataset
source_authors: Liu, Yawen
source_subjects: Oryza sativa
source_abstract: Abstract This repository contains the core datasets supporting the RiceMind platform, a comprehensive, structurally standardized, and fine-grained knowledge dataset for rice ( Oryza sativa ). To address the explosive growth of rice-related scientific literature, we employed automated, large-scale Natural Language Processing (NLP) strategies to mine experimentally validated associations from full-text articles (PubMed/PMC). This dataset not only provides extensive text-mined evidence for Gene-Trait Associations (GTAs), Gene-Variant Associations (GVAs), and Trait-Variant Associations (TVAs), but also seamlessly integrates these findings with multi-dimensional omics data and standardized ontologies. It serves as a robust resource for researchers in plant genomics, molecular breeding, and bioinformatics. Data Standardization & Identifier Mapping To ensure the highest level of structural consistency and cross-database interoperability, rigorous standardization pipelines were applied: Phenotypic Trait Standardization: All extracted trait descriptions have been systematically mapped and unified to recognized semantic ontologies, including the Gene Ontology (GO) , Plant Trait Ontology (TO) , Plant Ontology (PO) , and the Rice Trait Ontology (RTO) . The dataset centers around Oryza sativa . Gene Nomenclature Standardization: Gene entities sourced from external databases including Oryzabase , RAP-DB , Ensembl Plants , and Planteome were standardized to the unified RAP ID system. For instance, genes from Oryzabase were anchored via their annotated RAP IDs, and data from Planteome were mapped using a "Protein-Gene-RAP ID" trajectory to ensure absolute nomenclature consistency across the repository. Data Records Overview The repository includes the following files: 1. Text Corpus & Evidence Data keyword_filtered_rice_sentences.jsonl : Raw, keyword-filtered sentence segments extracted from full-text scientific literature. This serves as the foundational text corpus for downstream NLP processing. rice_context_sentences_compressed.tsv : Compressed contextual sentences providing the exact narrative evidence and semantic context from which the associations were mined. 2. NLP-Extracted Association Databases NLP_Rice_GTA_Database.tsv : The core text-mined Gene-Trait Association (GTA) dataset. It contains fine-grained, explicitly described relationships between rice genes and phenotypic traits extracted via automated NLP pipelines. NLP_Rice_GVA_TVA_Database.tsv : A supplementary association database capturing Gene-Variant Associations (GVAs) and Trait-Variant Associations (TVAs), mapping the genetic variations to specific traits and gene loci. NLP_Rice_GTA_Trend.tsv : Statistical and temporal trend data of the mined GTAs, reflecting the historical accumulation and rapid growth of specific rice breeding knowledge over time. 3. Integration & Standardization Masters Unified_Gene_Master.json : A comprehensive and standardized gene dictionary/ontology file. It resolves synonym conflicts and provides unified nomenclature for rice genes used across the entire dataset. rice_multi_omics.json : High-dimensional multi-omics data structures integrated to support and cross-validate the literature-mined narrative knowledge. Unified_Rice_GTA_Database.tsv : The definitive, ready-to-use master database. This file merges the NLP-extracted GTA dataset with the standardized gene master and multi-omics data layers, providing a fully integrated knowledge graph for downstream analysis. 4. NLP Terminology & Dictionaries terminology.tar.gz : A compressed archive containing a comprehensive collection of highly curated dictionaries ( *_oger_dict.tsv ) used for Named Entity Recognition (NER) and entity normalization in our NLP pipeline. All extracted dictionary files standardize entities into a strict 6-column format: [1] Source , [2] Label , [3] Unique Ontology ID , [4] Name , [5] Normalized Form , and [6] Entity Type . The terminology covers three main categories: Genes: Includes standard genes curated from Oryzabase ( oryzabase_gene_oger_dict.tsv ) and a supplementary gene list constructed via our NLP methods ( supplementary_gene_oger_dict.tsv ). Varieties: Standardized rice varieties and accessions compiled from the 3000 Rice Genomes Project ( variety_oger_dict.tsv ). Traits/Phenotypes: Comprehensive trait dictionaries mapped to established ontology systems, including Gene Ontology (GO, go_oger_dict.tsv ), Trait Ontology (TO, to_oger_dict.tsv ), Rice Trait Ontology (RTO, rto_oger_dict.tsv ), Crop Ontology 320 (CO_320, co_oger_dict.tsv ), and Plant Ontology (PO). Usage Notes Files ending in .tsv are tab-separated values and can be opened with standard data science libraries (e.g., pandas in Python or readr in R). Files ending in .json and .jsonl contain structured hierarchical data suitable for programmatic parsing.

For instance, genes from Oryzabase were anchored via their annotated RAP IDs, and data from Planteome were mapped using a "Protein-Gene-RAP ID" trajectory to ensure absolute nomenclature consistency across the repository. Data Records Overview The repository includes the following files: 1. Text Corpus & Evidence Data keyword_filtered_rice_sentences.jsonl : Raw, keyword-filtered sentence segments extracted from full-text scientific literature. This serves as the foundational text corpus for downstream NLP processing. rice_context_sentences_compressed.tsv : Compressed contextual sentences providing the exact narrative evidence and semantic context from which the associations were mined. 2. NLP-Extracted Association Databases NLP_Rice_GTA_Database.tsv : The core text-mined Gene-Trait Association (GTA) dataset. It contains fine-grained, explicitly described relationships between rice genes and phenotypic traits extracted via automated NLP pipelines. NLP_Rice_GVA_TVA_Database.tsv : A supplementary association database capturing Gene-Variant Associations (GVAs) and Trait-Variant Associations (TVAs), mapping the genetic variations to specific traits and gene loci. NLP_Rice_GTA_Trend.tsv : Statistical and temporal trend data of the mined GTAs, reflecting the historical accumulation and rapid growth of specific rice breeding knowledge over time. 3. Integration & Standardization Masters Unified_Gene_Master.json : A comprehensive and standardized gene dictionary/ontology file. It resolves synonym conflicts and provides unified nomenclature for rice genes used across the entire dataset. rice_multi_omics.json : High-dimensional multi-omics data structures integrated to support and cross-validate the literature-mined narrative knowledge. Unified_Rice_GTA_Database.tsv : The definitive, ready-to-use master database. This file merges the NLP-extracted GTA dataset with the standardized gene master and multi-omics data layers, providing a fully integrated knowledge graph for downstream analysis. 4. NLP Terminology & Dictionaries terminology.tar.gz : A compressed archive containing a comprehensive collection of highly curated dictionaries ( *_oger_dict.tsv ) used for Named Entity Recognition (NER) and entity normalization in our NLP pipeline. All extracted dictionary files standardize entities into a strict 6-column format: [1] Source , [2] Label , [3] Unique Ontology ID , [4] Name , [5] Normalized Form , and [6] Entity Type . The terminology covers three main categories: Genes: Includes standard genes curated from Oryzabase ( oryzabase_gene_oger_dict.tsv ) and a supplementary gene list constructed via our NLP methods ( supplementary_gene_oger_dict.tsv ). Varieties: Standardized rice varieties and accessions compiled from the 3000 Rice Genomes Project ( variety_oger_dict.tsv ). Traits/Phenotypes: Comprehensive trait dictionaries mapped to established ontology systems, including Gene Ontology (GO, go_oger_dict.tsv ), Trait Ontology (TO, to_oger_dict.tsv ), Rice Trait Ontology (RTO, rto_oger_dict.tsv ), Crop Ontology 320 (CO_320, co_oger_dict.tsv ), and Plant Ontology (PO). Usage Notes Files ending in .tsv are tab-separated values and can be opened with standard data science libraries (e.g., pandas in Python or readr in R). Files ending in .json and .jsonl contain structured hierarchical data suitable for programmatic parsing.

source_abstract: Набір даних містить результати польових досліджень щодо динаміки формування висоти рослин двох гібридів сорго зернового — Брігга та Ютамі — у різні фенологічні фази: повні сходи, кущення, вихід в трубку, викидання волоті, цвітіння та повна стиглість зерна. Досліджувались варіанти без мікродобрив та із застосуванням мікродобрив Альфа-Гроу-Екстра і Інтермаг у поєднанні з регуляторами росту Регоплант і Стимпо (або без них). Висота рослин гібрида Брігга у фазі повної стиглості зерна коливалася в межах 118,5–124,8 см, гібрида Ютамі — 111,1-117,2 см. Застосування мікродобрива Альфа-Гроу-Екстра у поєднанні зі Стимпо забезпечувало найвищі показники висоти рослин у обох гібридів на фінальних фазах розвитку. Роки досліджень 2019-2021.

source_title: AMARANTH (AMARANTHUS L.) AS A FUNCTIONAL CROP: BOTANICAL CHARACTERISTICS, NUTRITIONAL PROFILE, AND THERAPEUTIC POTENTIAL IN GASTROINTESTINAL DISORDERS
source_authors: Muzaffarova Nigora Safarovna
source_abstract: Background:  Amaranth (Amaranthus L.) is an ancient crop with significant nutritional and pharmacological properties. In recent decades, it has attracted global attention due to its high protein content, essential amino acids, and bioactive compounds with potential therapeutic effects. Objective:  This study aims to systematically evaluate the botanical characteristics, geographical distribution, nutritional composition, and therapeutic significance of Amaranthus species, with particular emphasis on their role in gastrointestinal health. Methods:  A comprehensive literature review was conducted using botanical, agronomic, and biomedical sources. Key species such as  Amaranthus caudatus ,  A. hybridus , and  A. retroflexus  were analyzed in terms of their biological, nutritional, and pharmacological properties. Results:  Amaranth demonstrates high nutritional value, including elevated protein content (14–19%), lysine-rich amino acid composition, and significant levels of polyphenols, dietary fiber, and squalene. These compounds exhibit antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and microbiota-modulating effects. Evidence suggests that amaranth contributes to improved gastrointestinal function, enhanced gut microbiota balance, and protection against digestive disorders. Conclusion: Amaranthus species represent a promising functional food and phytotherapeutic resource. Their bioactive compounds support potential applications in the prevention and treatment of gastrointestinal diseases. Further clinical studies are required to validate their therapeutic efficacy.

source_title: Genome Annotation files for Dillenia Suffruticosa
source_authors: Lim, Abner
source_subjects: Genome annotation; Plant Genomics; Dillenia suffruticosa
source_abstract: This dataset contains the structural genome annotation for Dillenia suffruticosa (Dilleniaceae), a tropical shrub native to Southeast Asia. The annotation was generated  using a combined ab initio and evidence-based approach, integrating computational gene prediction with supporting biological evidence to improve gene model accuracy and completeness. Four files are provided: FASTA ( Dsuffruticosa_v1.0.genome.fasta.gz ) - Dillenia suffruticosa Genome Assembly in FASTA format. GFF3 ( Dsuffruticosa_v1.0.gff3 ) — Structural annotation in GFF3 format, containing gene, mRNA, exon, and CDS feature coordinates mapped to the assembly scaffolds/chromosomes.  CDS FASTA ( Dsuffruticosa_v1.0_cds.fa ) — Nucleotide sequences of all predicted coding sequences, extracted based on the GFF3 coordinates. Headers correspond to transcript identifiers in the GFF3 file. Translated peptide FASTA ( Dsuffruticosa_v1.0_pep.fa ) — Amino acid sequences translated from the CDS features.

source_title: METHODS OF PROCESSING GRAPES FOR THE PRODUCTION OF FUNCTIONAL DRINKS
source_authors: Zaripov G.T; Ruzieva Z.A; Mirzaeva Sh.U
source_abstract: The article describes technological methods for processing grape berries and secondary products of their processing. An important source of biologically active substances is grape pomace, seeds, and skins, which contain a significant number of essential compounds. From grape pomace, tartaric acid salts, CO₂ extracts, grape oil, resveratrol, and plant-based flour are obtained. An improved structural scheme for producing clarified grape juice using CO₂ detartrating has been developed. A process flow diagram for grape processing has been designed. The chemical composition of grape seeds cultivated in the Republic of Uzbekistan has been studied. The content of resveratrol in a CO₂ extract obtained from grape skins has been determined. The amino acid composition of grape seed cake from the red Aleatico variety, obtained using the CO₂ method, has been analyzed.
